content: Why can the same compound figure be decomposed in more than one valid way?
instructor_notes: Require an individual prediction before discussion.

blocks.title: decompose figures and compute area accurately
content: Area is additive for nonoverlapping pieces.
Choose rectangles, triangles, and circles that minimize unknown dimensions.

blocks.title: Model the Skill: decompose figures and compute area accurately
content: A 15-by-10 rectangle has a 5-by-4 corner removed. Find the remaining area two ways.
verification: Verify all compound-area arithmetic and units.
steps: An additive decomposition of the same region also totals 130 square units.
The result is less than the 150-square-unit bounding rectangle.

blocks.title: You Try: decompose figures and compute area accurately
content: Find the area of a 12-by-9 rectangle with a 4-by-3 corner removed.
instructor_notes: Pause before revealing the solution.

blocks.title: Check and Diagnose: decompose figures and compute area accurately
content: Label units as square units.
Check that the result is smaller than the bounding rectangle.
instructor_notes: Ask students to explain why the incorrect path fails.
verification: Verify all compound-area arithmetic and units.

blocks.title: Make It Stick: decompose figures and compute area accurately
content: Describe two valid decomposition strategies for a compound region.

blocks.title: Predict: use circle terminology and circumference-area formulas
content: If a radius doubles, by what factor do circumference and area change?
instructor_notes: Require an individual prediction before discussion.

blocks.title: use circle terminology and circumference-area formulas
content: Circumference: $C=2\pi r$.
Area: $A=\pi r^2$.
A sector is bounded by two radii and an arc; a segment is bounded by a chord and arc.

blocks.title: Model the Skill: use circle terminology and circumference-area formulas
content: Compare radii 3 and 6, then find the annulus area between them.
verification: Verify circle and annulus formulas and results.
steps: Circumference changes from $6\pi$ to $12\pi$, so it doubles.
Area changes from $9\pi$ to $36\pi$, so it quadruples.
The annulus area is $36\pi-9\pi=27\pi$ square units.

blocks.title: You Try: use circle terminology and circumference-area formulas
content: A washer has outer radius 8 and inner radius 5. Find its exact area.
instructor_notes: Pause before revealing the solution.

blocks.title: Check and Diagnose: use circle terminology and circumference-area formulas
content: Use radius, not diameter, in formulas.
Subtract circle areas, not radii, for an annulus.
instructor_notes: Ask students to explain why the incorrect path fails.
verification: Verify circle and annulus formulas and results.

blocks.title: Make It Stick: use circle terminology and circumference-area formulas
content: Explain why circle area scales quadratically while circumference scales linearly.

blocks.title: Predict: apply central-angle, inscribed-angle, chord, and arc relationships
content: How does an intercepted arc compare with its central angle and an inscribed angle?
instructor_notes: Require an individual prediction before discussion.

blocks.title: apply central-angle, inscribed-angle, chord, and arc relationships
content: A central angle has the same measure as its intercepted arc.
An inscribed angle measures half its intercepted arc.
Equal chords intercept equal arcs.
Angles formed by intersecting chords inside a circle use half the sum of the intercepted arcs.

blocks.title: Model the Skill: apply central-angle, inscribed-angle, chord, and arc relationships
content: Use a central angle of 72° and its minor arc; then find an inscribed angle intercepting a 110° arc and a chord angle intercepting arcs 80° and 40°.
verification: Verify every circle theorem against its diagram.
steps: The central angle and minor arc are both 72°.
Locate the vertex first; the vertex determines which circle-angle rule applies.

blocks.title: You Try: apply central-angle, inscribed-angle, chord, and arc relationships
content: A central angle and an inscribed angle intercept the same minor arc. If the central angle is 86°, find the arc measure and the inscribed angle.
An inscribed angle measures 37°. Find its intercepted arc.
instructor_notes: Pause before revealing the solution.
answer: The minor arc is 86°; the inscribed angle is half of that, 43°.

blocks.title: Check and Diagnose: apply central-angle, inscribed-angle, chord, and arc relationships
content: Identify the vertex location before choosing a theorem.
Do not confuse central and inscribed angles.
instructor_notes: Ask students to explain why the incorrect path fails.
verification: Verify every circle theorem against its diagram.

blocks.title: Make It Stick: apply central-angle, inscribed-angle, chord, and arc relationships
content: Use vertex location to decide whether the intercepted arc matches a central angle or is twice an inscribed angle.

blocks.title: Predict: convert angle measures and compute arc length and sector area
content: Why must the angle be in radians when using $s=r\theta$?
instructor_notes: Require an individual prediction before discussion.

blocks.title: convert angle measures and compute arc length and sector area
content: Radians measure arc length per radius.
$s=r\theta$ and $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta$ require radians.
For inverse problems, solve $r=s/\theta$ or $\theta=2A/r^2$ before substituting.
Convert degrees using $\theta_{rad}=\theta_{deg}\pi/180$.

blocks.title: Model the Skill: convert angle measures and compute arc length and sector area
content: For $r=12$ and $\theta=120^\circ$, find arc length and sector area.
verification: Verify all degree-radian, arc-length, and sector-area calculations.

blocks.title: You Try: convert angle measures and compute arc length and sector area
content: Find the arc length for radius 9 and central angle 40°.
An arc has length $6\pi$ units and central angle $2\pi/5$ radians. Solve for the radius.
A sector has radius 5 units and area $25\pi/6$ square units. Find its central angle in radians and degrees.
Convert 135° to radians.
Convert $67.425^\circ$ to DMS and $22^\circ18'36''$ to decimal degrees.
instructor_notes: Ask students to name the unknown before choosing an equation.
For DMS, use 60 seconds per minute and 60 minutes per degree; pause before revealing solutions.

blocks.title: Check and Diagnose: convert angle measures and compute arc length and sector area
content: Do not insert degrees directly into radian formulas.
For an arc, isolate $r=s/\theta$ when radius is unknown; for a sector, isolate $\theta=2A/r^2$.
Sector area should be the same fraction of $\pi r^2$ as the angle is of a full rotation.
instructor_notes: Ask students to explain why the incorrect path fails.
verification: Verify all degree-radian, arc-length, and sector-area calculations.

blocks.title: Make It Stick: convert angle measures and compute arc length and sector area
content: Explain how you would recover a radius from arc length and angle, then recover a central angle from sector area and radius.
instructor_notes: If more than 3 minutes behind, shorten discussion but preserve the next practice and feedback slides.

blocks.title: Predict: relate angular velocity, linear velocity, and distance
content: Why do points farther from the center move faster even when angular speed is the same?
instructor_notes: Require an individual prediction before discussion.

blocks.title: relate angular velocity, linear velocity, and distance
content: Angular speed: $\omega=\theta/t$.
Linear speed: $v=r\omega$.
Distance: $d=vt=r\theta$.
For rpm, multiply by 360°/60 to get degrees per second; use 2π/60 to get radians per second for $v=rω$.

blocks.title: Model the Skill: relate angular velocity, linear velocity, and distance
content: A paddle tip at radius 4 ft rotates at 3 rad/s. Find speed and distance in 10 s.
verification: Verify angular-linear velocity examples and units.
steps: Radians are dimensionless in the linear-speed conversion.

blocks.title: You Try: relate angular velocity, linear velocity, and distance
content: A wheel of radius 0.35 m turns at 8 rad/s. Find rim speed.
A wheel of radius 3 ft turns at 18 revolutions per minute. Find angular speed in degrees per second and rim speed in feet per second.
instructor_notes: Require units in both the converted angular speed and linear speed.
Pause before revealing the two solutions.

blocks.title: Check and Diagnose: relate angular velocity, linear velocity, and distance
content: Angular units must be radians for $v=r\omega$.
For rev/min, convert to degrees per second with 360/60 and radians per second with 2π/60 before using $v=rω$.
Check that linear speed units include distance per time.
instructor_notes: Ask students to explain why the incorrect path fails.
verification: Verify angular-linear velocity examples and units.

blocks.title: Make It Stick: relate angular velocity, linear velocity, and distance
content: Describe how to convert rpm to degrees per second and radians per second, then use radius to find rim speed.

blocks.title: Predict: select volume and surface-area formulas for solids
content: Which dimensions contribute to volume, and which surfaces contribute to surface area?
instructor_notes: Require an individual prediction before discussion.

blocks.title: select volume and surface-area formulas for solids
content: Volume measures three-dimensional capacity; surface area measures exposed two-dimensional faces.
Cylinder: $V=\pi r^2h$ and $SA=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$.

blocks.title: Model the Skill: select volume and surface-area formulas for solids
content: A 10-unit pipe has outer radius 4 and inner radius 3. Find material volume.
verification: Verify all solid-geometry formulas, dimensions, and units.
steps: Subtract the inner cylinder from the outer cylinder.

blocks.title: You Try: select volume and surface-area formulas for solids
content: Find the volume of a cylinder with radius 3 and height 10, then its total surface area.
instructor_notes: Pause before revealing the solution.

blocks.title: Check and Diagnose: select volume and surface-area formulas for solids
content: Use cubic units for volume and square units for area.
A pipe requires outer volume minus inner volume.
instructor_notes: Ask students to explain why the incorrect path fails.
verification: Verify all solid-geometry formulas, dimensions, and units.

blocks.title: Make It Stick: select volume and surface-area formulas for solids
content: Explain how a diagram determines whether to add, subtract, or omit circular bases.

blocks.title: Circle, Radian, and Speed Review

blocks.title: Today’s practice sequence
content: Read the circle diagram
Convert the angle and keep precision
Find the unknown in an arc or sector
Convert rpm and use the radius

blocks.title: Where is the vertex?
content: Locate O and B. Which angle is central and which is inscribed?

assets.alt: Circle centered at O. Central angle AOD is 124 degrees. Point B lies outside the minor arc AD, with chords BA and BD. Find angle ABD and minor arc AD.
assets.caption: O is the center. Both angles intercept arc AD.

blocks.title: Angles and intercepted arcs
content: A central angle equals the measure of its intercepted arc.
An inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc.
All arcs around a circle total 360°.

assets.alt: Circle centered at O. Central angle AOD is 124 degrees. Point B lies outside the minor arc AD, with chords BA and BD. Find angle ABD and minor arc AD.
assets.caption: O is the center. Both angles intercept arc AD.

blocks.title: Central and inscribed angles
content: Find angle ABD and minor arc AD.
steps: The central angle AOD is 124°, so minor arc AD is 124°.
Angle ABD intercepts that same arc: $124^\circ/2=62^\circ$.
The vertex location determines the rule.

assets.alt: Circle centered at O. Central angle AOD is 124 degrees. Point B lies outside the minor arc AD, with chords BA and BD. Find angle ABD and minor arc AD.
assets.caption: O is the center. Both angles intercept arc AD.

blocks.title: Triangle and arc practice
content: Find angle BAC and minor arc BC.
Show the intermediate arc or triangle-angle calculation.

assets.alt: Triangle ABC inscribed in a circle. Minor arc AB is 78 degrees and angle ABC is 66 degrees. Find angle BAC and minor arc BC.
assets.caption: Given: arc AB = 78° and angle ABC = 66°.

instructor_notes: Packet page 1. Collect an individual setup before discussion.

blocks.title: Two routes to the same angle
content: Arc route: double the inscribed angle, subtract known arcs from 360°, then halve the remaining arc.
Triangle route: angle ACB is 39°, so angle BAC is 180° − 66° − 39° = 75°.
instructor_notes: Annotate the same figure; do not introduce intersecting-chord arithmetic today.

blocks.title: Circle-angle checkpoint
content: Name the vertex and intercepted arc before calculating.
Central angle = arc. Inscribed angle = half the arc.
blocks.pacing_checkpoint: Use the elapsed-time target to protect independent practice.

blocks.title: Which conversion is needed?
content: What changes when an angle is written as DMS, decimal degrees, or radians?
Which form is required in $s=r\theta$?

blocks.title: Angle conversion rules
content: $1^\circ=60\prime$ and $1\prime=60\prime\prime$.
DMS to decimal: $D+M/60+S/3600$.
Degrees to radians: multiply by $\pi/180$.
Radians to degrees: multiply by $180/\pi$.

blocks.title: Decimal degrees to DMS
content: Convert 38.726145° to DMS, to the nearest second.
steps: Degrees: 38°. Multiply the decimal part by 60: $0.726145(60)=43.5687$.
Minutes: 43′. Multiply the remaining decimal by 60: $0.5687(60)=34.122$.
instructor_notes: Keep all calculator digits until seconds. If rounding produces 60 seconds, carry one minute.

blocks.title: DMS to decimal degrees
content: Convert 101°18′24.7″ to decimal degrees, to four decimal places.

blocks.title: Decimal degrees to radians
content: Convert 137.6° to radians, to three decimal places.
steps: Keep π in the calculator expression. Round the final answer: 2.402 rad.

blocks.title: Conversion practice
content: Convert 58.417862° to DMS, to the nearest second.
Convert 112°36′18.5″ to decimal degrees, to four decimal places.
instructor_notes: Packet page 2. If time is short, students finish the second conversion immediately after class.

blocks.title: Precision and notation
content: Minutes and seconds use base 60. A decimal degree is not DMS notation.
Match the question’s requested decimal places. Round the final result once.

blocks.title: Conversion checkpoint
content: DMS to decimal uses division by 60 and 3600.
Decimal to DMS uses the fractional part twice, multiplying by 60.
blocks.pacing_checkpoint: Use the elapsed-time target to protect independent practice.

blocks.title: Length or area?
content: The same radius and angle determine both a curved distance and a shaded area.
Which quantity uses square units?

assets.alt: A circular sector with radius 6 units and central angle 1.4 radians. The curved boundary is marked s and the region A.
assets.caption: The curved boundary is a length; the shaded region is an area.

blocks.title: Arc and sector formulas
content: Arc length: $s=r\theta$. Sector area: $A=\tfrac12r^2\theta$.
Both formulas require θ in radians.
Unknown radius: $r=s/\theta$.
Unknown sector angle: $\theta=2A/r^2$, then convert to degrees if requested.

blocks.title: One sector, two measurements
content: Radius = 6 units and angle = 1.4 rad. Find arc length and sector area.
steps: The radius is squared only in the area formula.

assets.alt: A circular sector with radius 6 units and central angle 1.4 radians. The curved boundary is marked s and the region A.
assets.caption: The curved boundary is a length; the shaded region is an area.

blocks.title: Solve backwards for radius
content: Together: an arc is 24 units long with central angle 80°. Find the radius.
Then independently: an arc is 21 units long with central angle 105°. Find the radius.
instructor_notes: Packet page 3. Model the first setup on the board; leave the second unrevealed for an individual attempt.

blocks.title: Solve backwards for angle
content: A sector has area 35.4 square units and radius 4 units. Find θ in radians and degrees.
steps: The angle is between π and 2π radians, so a sector larger than a semicircle is reasonable.

assets.alt: A sector larger than a semicircle has radius 4 units and area 35.4 square units. Its central angle is unknown.
assets.caption: The highlighted sector can have an angle above 180°.

blocks.title: Check an inverse-sector setup
content: Without looking at the model, write an equation for a sector with area 35.4 and radius 4.
Solve for the angle in radians and degrees.
Explain why an angle above 180° is allowed.
answer: A sector can cover more than half a circle while remaining below a full 360° turn.

assets.alt: A sector larger than a semicircle has radius 4 units and area 35.4 square units. Its central angle is unknown.
assets.caption: The highlighted sector can have an angle above 180°.

instructor_notes: This is a retrieval attempt on the same numbers, not a second new example. Use the packet space to check algebra and units.

blocks.title: Check the setup before arithmetic
content: For radius, divide arc length by the angle in radians.
For angle, double the sector area and divide by the squared radius.
A 150° sector with radius 20 has area $500\pi/3\approx523.60$ square units.
instructor_notes: The final comparison corrects the legacy sprinkler example. Show the fraction-of-circle check: (150/360)π(20²). If behind, make this a quick oral check.

blocks.title: Arc and sector checkpoint
content: Circle the requested unknown first.
Convert degrees to radians before substitution.
Check whether the answer is a length, an area, or an angle.
blocks.pacing_checkpoint: Use the elapsed-time target to protect independent practice.

blocks.title: Same rotation, different distance
content: Do the center and the rim have the same angular speed?
Does a point farther from the center travel farther per turn?

blocks.title: From rpm to speed
content: Use radius = diameter ÷ 2.
Degrees per second: $n\cdot360/60$.
Radians per second: $\omega=n\cdot2\pi/60$.
Linear speed: $v=r\omega$ in distance units per second.

blocks.title: A rotating wheel
content: Diameter = 12 ft, rotation = 24 rpm. Find angular speed in degrees/s and rim speed in ft/s.

assets.alt: A wheel with diameter 12 feet makes 24 revolutions per minute. Find angular speed in degrees per second and rim speed in feet per second.
assets.caption: The given length crosses the entire wheel.

blocks.title: Rotation practice
content: A wheel has diameter 8 ft and turns at 30 rpm.
Find angular speed in degrees/s and linear speed at the rim in ft/s.
Write the diameter-to-radius step and both unit conversions.
instructor_notes: Packet page 4. Protect an individual attempt even if earlier discussion runs long.

blocks.title: Two common speed errors
content: Using the diameter in $v=r\omega$ doubles the speed.
Degrees/s cannot go directly into $v=r\omega$; use radians/s.
Convert minutes to seconds once, and label the final units.

blocks.title: Speed checkpoint
content: Radius first. Convert rpm. Then multiply radius by radians per second.
A sensible answer includes a distance unit and a time unit.

For Test 2 practice, compute arcs and sectors, convert angle measures, and relate angular and linear speed.

blocks.title: Cylinders: Volume and Surface Area
content: Wednesday, October 21, 2026 · 30-minute solids lesson after the 15-minute DMS-only Quiz 8
instructor_notes: Administer and collect the paper quiz before beginning this lesson.

blocks.title: Today’s sequence
content: Quiz 8 · 15 minutes · decimal degrees → DMS only
Lesson · distinguish capacity from exposed surface
Model and practice closed-cylinder volume and total surface area
Extend to material volume in a hollow cylinder

blocks.title: Capacity or covering?
content: A sealed can holds a drink and is painted over every outside surface, including both circular ends. Which measurement describes the drink it can hold? Which describes the paint needed?
instructor_notes: Have every student name the quantity and its unit before taking responses.

blocks.title: Cylinder volume and surface-area formulas
content: Base area and circumference: $A_{\mathrm{base}}=\pi r^2$, $C=2\pi r$.
Volume (capacity): $V=A_{\mathrm{base}}h=\pi r^2h$. Units are cubic.
Lateral area (curved side): $LA=Ch=2\pi rh$.
Closed total surface: $SA=2A_{\mathrm{base}}+LA$ (two bases plus curved side).
Expanded form: $SA=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$. Units are square.

assets.alt: A closed cylinder beside its three surface parts: two matching circular ends and one rectangular curved-side piece, shown in matching colors.
assets.caption: Two circular ends plus one curved side make the closed-cylinder surface.

instructor_notes: Point to each surface part as its term appears. For an open cylinder, include only the surfaces that are present.

blocks.title: Model: diameter given, radius required
content: A closed cylinder has diameter $d=10$ cm and height $h=8$ cm. Find exact and approximate volume and total surface area.
steps: The given measure is the diameter, so $r=d/2=10/2=5$ cm.
Two bases: $2\pi r^2=50\pi\text{ cm}^2$. Curved side: $LA=2\pi rh=80\pi\text{ cm}^2$.

assets.alt: A closed cylinder with one measurement line across the full top diameter and another alongside its full height.
assets.caption: The top line spans the full diameter; the side line marks height.

instructor_notes: Pause after the radius conversion; have students predict which result needs square units and which needs cubic units.

blocks.title: You try: closed-cylinder volume and area
content: A closed cylinder has radius $r=3$ cm and height $h=10$ cm. Find exact and approximate volume and total surface area. Show the two surface-area contributions.
answer: Two bases: $2\pi(3)^2=18\pi\text{ cm}^2$; curved side: $2\pi(3)(10)=60\pi\text{ cm}^2$.

assets.alt: A single closed cylinder shown in three-quarter view, with its circular base and curved side visible.
assets.caption: Use the radius for the circular base and the height for the cylinder's length.

instructor_notes: Give students quiet think time before comparing setups.
blocks.pacing_checkpoint: At 17 minutes into the teaching block, check whether radius and unit choices are secure.

blocks.title: Check the setup before the arithmetic
content: Use the radius in both formulas; when the problem gives diameter, divide it by two first.
Volume uses cubic units. Surface area uses square units and counts only the surfaces that are present.

blocks.title: Extension: material in a hollow cylinder
content: A pipe segment has outer radius $R=4$ cm, inner radius $r=3$ cm, and length $h=10$ cm. Find the volume of material.
steps: The material cross-section is an annulus: $A_{\mathrm{material}}=\pi R^2-\pi r^2=\pi(R^2-r^2)$.
Subtract the inner circle's area, not the radii; volume uses cubic units.

assets.alt: A hollow cylindrical pipe segment with a clearly visible annular cut end around an open inner bore.
assets.caption: The blue ring is material; the orange opening is the inner volume removed.

instructor_notes: Name the outer and inner radii before substituting; the inner radius describes the hollow opening.
blocks.pacing_checkpoint: At 23 minutes into teaching, protect the exit check and use the remaining five minutes as flex.

blocks.title: Exit check: what is being measured?
content: A closed cylinder has $r=3$ cm and $h=7$ cm. One student labels its capacity $63\pi$ cm$^2$ and its total surface area $60\pi$ cm$^3$. Identify and correct the mix-up.
answer: Capacity is volume: $63\pi$ cm$^3$. Total surface area is $60\pi$ cm$^2$. The student switched both the quantities and their units.
Keep the final five minutes flexible for completion, correction, or a second radius-versus-diameter check.
